flashcards.q: What is the low-link value low[u] and what mechanism does it enable?
flashcards.a: The minimum of disc[u], low[v] for tree children v, and disc[w] for back-edge ancestors w -- it's the mechanism behind SCC roots, bridges, and articulation points, all derived from the same single DFS pass.

flashcards.q: What is Tarjan's condition for a vertex being the root of a completed SCC?
flashcards.a: low[v] == disc[v] -- nothing in v's subtree can reach any ancestor earlier than v, so the stack down to v is one complete, maximal SCC.

flashcards.q: State the exact bridge condition and the exact non-root articulation point condition, and why they differ (strict vs non-strict).
flashcards.a: Bridge: low[v] > disc[u] (strict) -- child's subtree has NO way back to u or beyond. Articulation point (non-root): low[v] >= disc[u] (non-strict) -- even reaching back to exactly u still means removing u disconnects that subtree from anything above u.

flashcards.q: What is the DFS root's special articulation-point condition, and why is it different from every other vertex?
flashcards.a: The root is an articulation point iff it has MORE THAN ONE DFS-tree child. The general condition relies on a parent/ancestor to reach around; the root has none, so removing it separates its children's subtrees from each other only if there are 2+ of them.

flashcards.q: How do you build the 2-SAT implication graph from clause (a OR b), and what's the unsatisfiability check?
flashcards.a: Add edges NOT a -> b and NOT b -> a. Formula is unsatisfiable iff some variable x and NOT x land in the same SCC (mutual implication = contradiction).

flashcards.q: Why is 2-SAT polynomial-time solvable while 3-SAT is NP-complete?
flashcards.a: A 2-literal clause translates cleanly into exactly 2 directed implication edges, giving a linear-size graph solvable via SCC. A 3-literal clause has no equivalent 2-edge representation, so the same technique doesn't apply, and no other polynomial reduction is known.

flashcards.q: Why is the condensation graph of SCCs always acyclic?
flashcards.a: If distinct SCCs formed a cycle in the condensation, every vertex in every SCC on that cycle could reach every other via chaining -- they'd all be mutually reachable and should have been one single SCC, contradicting maximality.

flashcards.q: Account Merging (LC 721): why is Union-Find the right tool here instead of Tarjan's SCC algorithm?
flashcards.a: The 'same person' relation is undirected/symmetric by nature, not a directed reachability question -- Union-Find is the conceptually correct match for an equivalence-class problem; reaching for SCC machinery here is pattern-matching without understanding what SCC actually measures.
